concepts.title: Astronomy: An Ancient Science Born of Wonder
concepts.definition: Astronomy studies the objects seen in the sky, and it is an ancient science -- perhaps as old as the day humans left their caves for the open. The phases of the moon, eclipses and other celestial phenomena drew wonder and awe, and that wonder grew into careful, regular observation.
concepts.key_idea: Wonder at the sky was the first laboratory -- watching moon and eclipses nightly made astronomy a science.

solution_steps.explain: Astronomy is the study of sky objects -- their motions and patterns.
Its data-collection began in prehistory, with moon phases and eclipses the most striking recurring events.
Repeated observation turned awe into prediction -- the birth of a science of the sky.

concepts.title: Indian Astronomical Tradition: Calendars and the Nakshatra Sky
concepts.definition: Indian astronomers mapped the sky into nakshatras -- lunar mansions -- and built calendars that tracked the sun and moon together, fixing festivals, seasons and agricultural timings. Eclipses, once feared, came to be calculated, showing the tradition's move from belief to computation.
concepts.key_idea: Stars became a calendar -- nakshatra tracks and sun-moon reckoning turned the sky into social time.

solution_steps.explain: The moon's monthly path was divided into nakshatra stations, giving a reference grid of stars.
Combining solar and lunar motions produced calendars -- tithis, months, festival dates, sowing seasons.
Understanding the moon's shadow geometry let astronomers calculate eclipses, replacing fear with prediction.

concepts.title: Astronomy in Service of Life
concepts.definition: Astronomy in India was never detached from life: it fixed the agricultural calendar, guided navigation and travel, and ordered ritual and social time. The same observations that satisfied wonder also served farms, festivals and journeys -- knowledge woven into society.
concepts.key_idea: Sky knowledge fed the field and the festival -- astronomy worked as society's clock and compass.

solution_steps.explain: Seasonal markers read from the sky told farmers when to sow and harvest.
Ritual dates, fixed astronomically, coordinated communities across regions.
Star positions guided journeys, making the same sky a compass as well as a clock.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain how the nakshatra division of the sky helped ancient astronomers keep track of time.

solution_template.explain: The moon's path was marked into nakshatra stations along the ecliptic.
Each night the moon sits near a known station, so its position reads off the date of the lunar month.
The sky thus functioned as a public calendar readable by trained observers.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A farmer in early India decides when to sow. Show how astronomical knowledge guided the decision.

solution_template.explain: The sun's shift into a known constellation and the moon's phase marked the season's turn.
Such markers preceded the rains regularly, so they served as a forecast.
Sowing timed to the sky tied agriculture to astronomy -- knowledge serving subsistence.
